angle: Reps got jealous of enterprise deals, emailed 40 people at one company in a week, and killed deliverability
post_first_line: 40 people at one company. One week.
linkedin_post:
40 people at one company. One week.

That's all it took to wreck deliverability for an entire team.

Here's what happened. A couple of reps saw the ticket price on enterprise deals and got jealous. Mid-market was working, but enterprise looked like where the real money was.

So they started sending, and not carefully. Sometimes to 40 different people at the same large company in the same week.

Then the data shifted. Enterprise recipients stopped receiving emails at the same rate they had before. We had clean prior history showing things were going well, and then a sudden break.

The dashboard couldn't explain why. We had to open up the actual sequences and look at what changed from a sending perspective.

The cause was behavior, not the list or the copy. A few reps changed how they sent, and it hurt deliverability.

When performance drops, don't just stare at the cohort metrics. Go read the sequences and see who is doing what.

What's the worst sending behavior you've had to untangle?

Slide 2: Reps saw enterprise ticket prices and got jealous
Slide 3: Mid-market worked, but enterprise looked more exciting
Slide 4: Sending patterns changed and enterprise emails stopped landing
Slide 5: Prior data showed things were going well before the break
Slide 6: The dashboard couldn't explain it, the sequences could
Slide 7: A few reps' sending behavior hurt deliverability

lesson.title: When deliverability drops, check rep behavior first
takeaways: Enterprise excitement can push reps to over-send to one account, such as 40 contacts in a week.
Cohort-level metrics show that something broke, not why.
Comparing prior good data against current sending behavior in the sequences reveals the cause.
lesson.exercise: Pull the last 30 days of sends and count how many people each rep emailed per account per week. Flag any account with an unusually high number and review those sequences.

angle: If your only email variable is first name, you have work to do.
post_first_line: 10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.
linkedin_post:
10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.

Most people think they've solved it with one merge field.

Copy variation matters for deliverability. Blasting the same email across thousands of recipients is exactly what you don't want to do.

So yes, I always recommend templated variables: first name, the mailbox you're sending from, and other details that change per send. Those mailboxes should be linked to sequences with copy that uses spin syntax or is uniquely generated.

Variation beats static every time, and variables are the easiest way to add some of it.

But here's my caveat: if your only variable is the recipient's first name, you have work to do.

First name is the floor, not the strategy.

When was the last time you audited your email variables?
carousel: Slide 1: If your only variable is first name, you have work to do.
Slide 2: Sending 10,000 identical emails hurts your deliverability.
Slide 3: Copy variation is better than static copy. Every time.
Slide 4: Variables are the easiest path to adding variation.
Slide 5: Template first name and the mailbox you send from.
Slide 6: Link mailboxes to sequences with spin syntax or unique copy.
Slide 7: First name alone is the floor, not the strategy.
Slide 8: Audit your variables before your next send.

lesson.title: First Name Is Not Personalization: Variation for Deliverability
takeaways: Sending thousands of identical emails is a deliverability risk, so copy variation protects your sending.
Variables like first name and sending mailbox are an easy way to add some variation.
Pair variables with sequences that use spin syntax or uniquely generated copy; first name alone isn't enough.
lesson.exercise: Pull up your active sequence and count the variables. If first name is the only one, add at least two more sources of variation, such as spin syntax or uniquely generated lines, before your next send.

angle: Who should own what when your cold email program starts slipping
post_first_line: Four teams own your cold email health.
linkedin_post:
Four teams own your cold email health.
Most companies assume one of them does.

When replies start slipping, the first problem is usually that nobody knows whose job it is to look. Here's how I think about the split.

Sales owns the sending plan. How many emails go out, and at the rep level, how you ramp people up to full volume.

RevOps owns list quality. Are the people you're sending to on legitimate mailboxes? And when replies drop, can you inspect which segments are actually taking the hit, instead of staring at one blended number?

IT owns domain setup. Are your domains authenticated properly and ready to send? IT is also the team that can answer the question, what changed?

Then there's the sending vendor. Someone has to check who is sending from which domains and whether those domains are actually healthy. That could be RevOps, or it could be deliverability if you have that in-house.

When a program slips, you don't want a debate about whose problem it is. You want four people who already know which lever is theirs.

Who owns domain health on your team today?
carousel: Slide 1: Four teams own your cold email health.
Slide 2: Sales owns the sending plan and rep-level ramp to full volume.
Slide 3: RevOps owns list quality and legitimate mailboxes.
Slide 4: RevOps also inspects which segments are dropping on replies.
Slide 5: IT owns domain setup and proper authentication.
Slide 6: IT also answers the question: what changed?
Slide 7: Someone must check which domains send, and if they're healthy.
Slide 8: Assign owners before replies slip, not after.

lesson.title: Assigning ownership across your cold email program
takeaways: Sales owns the sending plan: volume and how each rep ramps to full volume.
RevOps owns list quality and can inspect which segments are causing a reply drop.
IT owns domain setup and authentication, and can answer what changed; someone must also monitor sending vendor and domain health.
lesson.exercise: Write down the four areas (sending plan, list quality, domain setup, sending vendor/domain health) and put one named owner next to each. Any blank is your risk.

caption: Who owns cold email health?

angle: New mailbox, reply rates tanked. You probably started sending too soon.
linkedin_post:
New mailbox. Reply rates tanked.

Before you blame the copy, check one thing first.

Most of the time, the finding is simple: we started sending too soon.

The mailbox wasn't ready for the volume we wanted to push through it. We matched our pipeline target, not the quality of the mailbox.

I know people have pipeline targets. But this is where deliverability gets granular. If the mailbox hasn't earned the volume, the sends don't land.

The fix is quick. Modify your daily sending volume.

Warm those new mailboxes further, ramp your actual sends more slowly, and adjust from there.

No rewriting the whole campaign. No new list. Just slow down the ramp.

What's your rule for ramping new mailboxes?
carousel: Slide 1: New mailbox, reply rates tanked? Check this first.
Slide 2: Before blaming copy, ask if you started sending too soon.
Slide 3: Pipeline targets don't set how much a mailbox can handle.
Slide 4: The mistake: matching sends to your goal, not mailbox quality.
Slide 5: The fix starts with lowering your daily sending volume.
Slide 6: Keep warming the new mailboxes for longer.
Slide 7: Ramp actual sends more slowly, then adjust from there.
Slide 8: Don't rewrite the campaign until the mailbox is ready.

lesson.title: Don't Outrun Your Mailbox
takeaways: When reply rates drop on a new mailbox, sending too soon is a likely culprit.
Sending volume should match the quality of the mailbox, not your pipeline target.
The quick fix is to warm the mailbox further and ramp sends more slowly.
lesson.exercise: Pull up your newest mailboxes. Cut daily send volume, set a slower weekly ramp, and compare reply rates after each step before changing any copy.

angle: 3 things to do this week to find out why your replies dropped
linkedin_post:
3 things to do this week.

Reply rates dropped, and a dashboard alone won't tell you why.

Here's what I'd do coming out of this webinar:

1. Review one or two of your emails. Look at how many links you're including, how many faux pas have crept in, and how much of the copy adds no value for the reader.

2. Run one split test against an existing sequence. Take your lead list, cut it in half, and test one change against the original.

3. Decide who owns the investigation when a drop happens. Name one person before it happens.

The drop alone doesn't tell you the full story. You have to see what changed at the same time as the drop.

Without an owner, nobody goes looking for that change.

Who owns reply-rate investigations on your team?
carousel: Slide 1: Replies dropped? Do these 3 things this week.
Slide 2: First, review one or two of your actual emails.
Slide 3: Count the links and the low-value copy.
Slide 4: Second, run one split test on an existing sequence.
Slide 5: Split your lead list in half and test it.
Slide 6: Third, name who owns the investigation when a drop happens.
Slide 7: The drop alone never tells you the full story.
Slide 8: Find what changed alongside the drop.

lesson.title: How to investigate a drop in reply rates
takeaways: Audit your emails for too many links, faux pas, and copy that adds no value.
Split test against an existing sequence by dividing your lead list in half.
Assign a clear owner for investigations, because the drop alone doesn't explain what changed.
lesson.exercise: Pick one live sequence this week. Review one email for links and low-value copy, split the lead list in half to test one change, and write down who owns the investigation if replies drop.

angle: Same 10,000 emails, 36 meetings vs 28: what inbox placement costs you
linkedin_post:
8 meetings. Same 10,000 emails.

The only thing that changed was where those emails landed.

Here's the illustrative math I walk through. One team gets a 90% placement rate, meaning emails actually reach the primary tab and inbox. Based on some assumptions about reply rates, 10,000 emails turns into 36 meetings.

Now change one variable. Same list, same copy, same volume. Only the share of emails reaching the inbox drops. Those 10,000 emails turn into 28 meetings.

That's a delta of 8 meetings.

Depending on your price point, that could be hundreds of thousands of ARR that never converts into deals.

Fewer emails in the inbox doesn't just mean worse metrics on a dashboard. It means fewer meetings and less revenue.

Most teams I talk to obsess over copy and sequencing. Placement quietly takes a cut before any of that matters.

When did you last check your inbox placement?
carousel: Slide 1: Same 10,000 emails. 36 meetings versus 28.
Slide 2: The only variable changed was inbox placement.
Slide 3: Team A: 90% placement, landing in primary and inbox.
Slide 4: Team A turns 10,000 emails into 36 meetings.
Slide 5: Team B reaches fewer inboxes with the same send.
Slide 6: Team B gets only 28 meetings from 10,000 emails.
Slide 7: An 8-meeting gap can mean hundreds of thousands in ARR.
Slide 8: Fewer emails in the inbox means less revenue.

lesson.title: Inbox placement is a revenue lever
takeaways: Fewer emails reaching the inbox means fewer meetings and less revenue.
In the illustrative example, the same 10,000 emails produced 36 meetings at 90% placement and 28 at lower placement.
Depending on price point, an 8-meeting gap could be hundreds of thousands of ARR.
lesson.exercise: Take your last 10,000 sends, estimate your inbox placement rate, and multiply the gap by your reply-to-meeting rate and average deal size to see what placement is costing you.

caption: Same emails. 8 fewer meetings.
